landmark-001.summary: An iron landmark built for the 1889 World's Fair, now the symbol of Paris, France, and of modern iron architecture.
facts: It was originally meant to be a temporary structure standing for only 20 years.
After dark, 20,000 lights sparkle for five minutes at the top of every hour.

landmark-002.summary: A monument Napoleon raised in Paris, France, to celebrate his victory at Austerlitz, with the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath it.
facts: Construction began in 1806 and finished in 1836, so Napoleon never saw it completed.
Climb its 284 steps and you'll see twelve grand avenues radiating out like a star.

landmark-003.summary: A former royal palace in Paris, France, opened to the public by the revolutionary government in 1793 and now the world's most-visited art museum.
facts: It is home to the “Mona Lisa” and the Venus de Milo.
Its glass pyramid entrance, opened in 1989, was designed by architect I. M. Pei.

landmark-004.summary: An abbey on a rocky tidal island off Normandy, France, dedicated to the Archangel Michael and a pilgrimage site since the Middle Ages.
facts: During the Hundred Years' War, it held out against an English siege to the very end.
The old causeway was removed and replaced with a bridge, so it becomes an island again at high spring tides.

landmark-005.summary: A great bell that has rung from the clock tower of the Houses of Parliament in London since 1859, a symbol of the city and of British parliamentary democracy.
facts: It weighs 13.7 tons and fell almost silent during a five-year restoration that began in 2017.
The tower's official name, Elizabeth Tower, was given in 2012 to mark the Queen's Diamond Jubilee.

landmark-006.summary: A Victorian drawbridge over the Thames in London, opened in 1894, whose lifting central span has made it a symbol of the city.
facts: It takes its name from the Tower of London, which stands right beside it.
Glass floors added to the upper walkways in 2014 let you look down at the river 42 meters below.

landmark-007.summary: A prehistoric ring of giant stones raised on Salisbury Plain in England around 2500 BC, thought to be a ceremonial and burial site and now a World Heritage Site.
facts: Visitors normally view it from behind a fence, but at dawn on the summer solstice they can walk among the stones to greet the sunrise.
Many of the smaller bluestones were hauled from Wales, more than 200 kilometers away.

landmark-008.summary: The official London residence of the British monarch since 1837, where state visits and royal ceremonies are held, and a symbol of the monarchy.
facts: The Changing of the Guard takes place in front of the main gates at 11 a.m., almost daily in summer.
When the monarch is in residence, the Royal Standard flies overhead.

landmark-009.summary: An amphitheatre built in Rome, Italy, around AD 80, where gladiators fought, and a lasting symbol of the might of the Roman Empire.
facts: It appears on Italy's 5-cent euro coin.
Emperor Titus opened it with 100 days of games.

landmark-010.summary: The campanile of a cathedral square in Tuscany, Italy, begun in 1173, which tilted on soft ground and became world-famous for it.
facts: Today you can climb 296 slanting steps up to the belfry at the top.
It closed in 1990 for 11 years of stabilization work that reduced its tilt from 5.5 to 4 degrees.

landmark-011.summary: A Baroque water monument completed in Rome, Italy, in 1762, centred on a statue of the sea god Oceanus and the largest of its kind in the city.
facts: Legend says tossing a coin over your shoulder ensures you'll return to Rome; the money collected goes to the charity Caritas.
It is still fed by the Aqua Virgo, an aqueduct built in 19 BC.

landmark-012.summary: The political and religious heart of the old Venetian Republic in Venice, Italy, where a Byzantine-style basilica faces the Doge's Palace.
facts: Napoleon is said to have called it “the most beautiful drawing room in Europe.”
Between fall and spring, high tides known as acqua alta flood the square.

landmark-013.summary: The seat of the archbishop in Lombardy's capital in northern Italy, the largest church in the country and a masterpiece of Gothic architecture.
facts: Construction began in 1386, and it was not officially completed until 1965.
With a ticket, you can go up to the rooftop terraces and stroll among the spires.

landmark-014.summary: An ancient Roman town near Naples, Italy, buried by the ash of Vesuvius in AD 79, preserving everyday life frozen in time and now a World Heritage Site.
facts: Stone shop counters with built-in food jars still line its streets.
Systematic excavation began in 1748.

landmark-015.summary: A church in Barcelona, Spain, begun in 1882, to which Gaudí devoted the last 40-odd years of his life, still under construction and a symbol of the city.
facts: Antoni Gaudí was struck by a tram and killed in 1926, never seeing it finished.
In February 2026, its central Tower of Jesus reached 172.5 meters, making it the tallest church in the world.

landmark-016.summary: The palace-fortress of the Nasrid dynasty on a hill in Granada, Spain, the last great masterpiece of Islamic culture in the Iberian Peninsula.
facts: After visiting, Francisco Tárrega composed the guitar piece “Recuerdos de la Alhambra.”
Its surrender by the last Muslim dynasty in 1492 marked the end of the Reconquista.

landmark-017.summary: A hillside garden complex in Barcelona, Spain, designed by Gaudí, where colourful tile mosaics and curving architecture earned it World Heritage status.
facts: It was originally planned as an upscale housing estate before becoming a park.
The tiled lizard on the entrance stairway, El Drac, is always crowded with people taking photos.

landmark-018.summary: A national gallery opened in Madrid, Spain, in 1819 from the royal collections, holding one of the world's finest collections of European painting.
facts: Its walls hold Diego Velázquez's “Las Meninas” and Goya's “The Third of May 1808.”
During the last two hours before closing, the permanent collection is free to visit.

landmark-019.summary: A 16th-century fortress guarding the mouth of the Tagus in Lisbon, Portugal, a Manueline symbol of the country's glory in the Age of Discovery.
facts: Ships setting out on the sea route to India sailed right past it.
In 1983, it became a World Heritage Site together with the Jerónimos Monastery.

landmark-020.summary: A neoclassical monument built in Berlin, Germany, in 1791, which witnessed the country's division and reunification and became a symbol of German unity.
facts: It appears on Germany's 10-, 20- and 50-cent euro coins.
In December 1989, the gate, long blocked by the Berlin Wall, reopened after 28 years.

landmark-021.summary: A Romantic royal residence that Ludwig II of Bavaria, a devoted admirer of Wagner's operas, built on an Alpine hill in southern Germany in the style of medieval legend.
facts: It was still unfinished when the king died in 1886, and it opened to visitors just seven weeks later.
It is often cited as the model for the Disney castle.

landmark-022.summary: A Gothic church on the Rhine in Germany that houses the Shrine of the Three Kings, making it a major pilgrimage site of medieval Europe and now a World Heritage Site.
facts: It took 14 bomb hits during World War II and still did not collapse.
With no elevator, visitors climb 533 steps to the south tower's viewing platform, about 100 meters up.

landmark-023.summary: The Baroque summer residence of the Habsburgs on the outskirts of Vienna, Austria, a World Heritage Site that reflects the splendour of their empire.
facts: It has 1,441 rooms, and its grounds hold the world's oldest zoo, opened in 1752.
In 1762, a six-year-old Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart performed for the empress in its Hall of Mirrors.

landmark-024.summary: A royal complex built from the 9th century on a hill above the Vltava in the Czech capital, the seat of power for more than a thousand years.
facts: Every day at noon, a grand Changing of the Guard takes place in the first courtyard by the main gate.
Once the seat of the kings of Bohemia, it now houses the office of the Czech president.

landmark-025.summary: A Gothic stone crossing begun in 1357 over the Vltava in Prague, Czech Republic, linking the Old Town to the castle along the coronation route of kings.
facts: Legend says touching the relief of St. John of Nepomuk on the bridge will make your wish come true.
Until 1841, it was the only bridge across the Vltava in Prague.

landmark-026.summary: A sanctuary of the goddess Athena built on the Acropolis of Athens, Greece, in the 5th century BC, a symbol of ancient Greek democracy and classical architecture.
facts: About half of its sculptures were removed in the early 19th century by the British diplomat Lord Elgin and are now in the British Museum.
Its columns bulge slightly in the middle so that they appear perfectly straight.

landmark-027.summary: A volcanic island in Greece's Cyclades in the Aegean, whose white houses lining the cliffs have become the classic image of Greek island travel.
facts: Around 1600 BC, a massive eruption collapsed the center of the island, leaving it crescent-shaped.
Every evening, crowds gather on the cliffs of Oia to watch the sunset.

landmark-028.summary: An onion-domed church built by Ivan IV on Red Square in Moscow, Russia, to celebrate the conquest of Kazan, and the country's most iconic building.
facts: Legend says the architect was blinded so he could never build anything like it again, but there is no evidence for this.
Its vivid colors are the result of repeated repainting from the 1680s to 1848.

landmark-029.summary: An art collection housed in the former Winter Palace of the Russian tsars in Saint Petersburg, one of the largest in the world.
facts: It began in 1764 with 225 paintings purchased by Catherine II.
Dozens of cats, first brought in to catch mice, still live in its basements.

landmark-030.summary: A cathedral built by the Byzantine emperor Justinian in Istanbul, Türkiye, in 537, the pinnacle of Byzantine architecture and a symbol of the meeting of East and West.
facts: It became a mosque in 1453 and a museum in 1935, then was converted back into a mosque in 2020.
Since January 2024, foreign tourists pay a 25-euro admission fee.

landmark-031.summary: A volcanic plateau in central Anatolia, Türkiye, where churches carved into the rock still hold early Christian frescoes, now a World Heritage Site.
facts: People carved underground cities out of rock formed from hardened volcanic ash.
Every morning at dawn, dozens of hot-air balloons rise into the sky together.

landmark-032.summary: A 4,478-metre peak on the border of Switzerland and Italy whose pyramid-like shape has made it the symbol of the Alps and of Switzerland.
facts: Until 2023, it was pictured on the packaging of Toblerone chocolate.
Edward Whymper's party of seven made the first ascent in 1865, but four of them died on the way down.

landmark-033.summary: A 4,158-metre snow-capped peak in Switzerland's Bernese Alps that, together with the surrounding glaciers, became the first natural World Heritage Site in the Alps.
facts: Opened in 1912, the station on the saddle sits at 3,454 meters, the highest railway station in Europe.
The Aletsch Glacier, the longest in the Alps, stretches out beside it.

landmark-034.summary: A church in Vatican City said to stand over the tomb of the apostle regarded as the first pope, the central pilgrimage site of the Catholic world.
facts: Michelangelo designed its dome, and Bernini designed the oval square in front of it.
At Easter and Christmas, the pope blesses the crowds in the square from the central balcony.

landmark-035.summary: The papal place of worship built inside the Vatican Palace in 1481, its walls covered with frescoes by Renaissance masters.
facts: Starting in 1508, Michelangelo spent four years painting its ceiling frescoes of the Creation.
During a conclave, white smoke rising from its chimney means a new pope has been elected.

landmark-036.summary: A bronze figure seated on a seaside rock in Copenhagen, Denmark, honouring Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale and a symbol of the city since 1913.
facts: Carl Jacobsen, son of the founder of Carlsberg, commissioned it after falling in love with a ballet based on the story.
Standing just 1.25 meters tall, it surprises many first-time visitors with its small size.

landmark-037.summary: A glacier-carved sea inlet in western Norway, with old mountain farms clinging to its cliffs, and the showpiece of the country's coastal scenery.
facts: On the opposite cliff stands the Suitor waterfall, facing the Sisters.
It was designated a World Natural Heritage Site in 2005.

landmark-038.summary: An open-air spa in a lava field in southwestern Iceland, filled with geothermal seawater from a power plant and now the country's best-known attraction.
facts: Since 2023, repeated eruptions from nearby volcanoes have forced it to close several times.
Its water looks blue because of the silica it contains.

landmark-039.summary: Medieval fortifications encircling the old city of the Republic of Ragusa on Croatia's Adriatic coast, guarding the "Pearl of the Adriatic", a World Heritage Site.
facts: You can walk a full loop along the top of the roughly 1,940-meter circuit.
It served as a filming location for King's Landing, the capital in the TV series “Game of Thrones.”

landmark-040.summary: The largest Nazi German forced-labour and extermination camp, in southern Poland, now a memorial museum bearing witness to the horrors of the Holocaust.
facts: At least 1.1 million people lost their lives here.
It was liberated by Soviet troops on January 27, 1945, a date now marked as International Holocaust Remembrance Day.

landmark-041.summary: A long defensive barrier built along mountain ridges by successive Chinese dynasties to hold back northern nomads, a World Heritage Site symbolising Chinese civilisation.
facts: Successive dynasties added to it, and most of what stands today dates from the Ming dynasty.
The Ming-era sections are usually said to run from Shanhai Pass in the east to Jiayu Pass in the west.

landmark-042.summary: The palace complex in the heart of Beijing, China, from which Ming and Qing emperors ruled for nearly 500 years, the symbol of imperial power.
facts: The Palace Museum was established here in 1925, so anyone with a ticket can walk through the palace.
Some 980 buildings survive; the claim that it has 9,999 rooms is an exaggeration.

landmark-043.summary: A host of clay soldiers and horses buried beside the tomb of the First Emperor of Qin near Xi'an, China, to guard him in the afterlife, a symbol of Qin military might.
facts: It was discovered in 1974 by farmers digging a well.
Every soldier has a different face.

landmark-044.summary: The residence of successive Dalai Lamas, built in tiers on the Red Hill of Lhasa, Tibet, and once the centre of Tibetan Buddhism and government.
facts: It stands at an altitude of about 3,700 meters.
It served as the winter palace of the Dalai Lamas until the 1959 exile.

landmark-045.summary: A white marble mausoleum built in Agra, India, by a Mughal emperor in memory of his late wife, the supreme masterpiece of Indo-Islamic architecture.
facts: Shah Jahan began it in 1632 and, with some 20,000 artisans, completed it in 1653.
It is closed to tourists on Fridays.

landmark-046.summary: The world's largest religious monument, built by the Khmer Empire near Siem Reap, Cambodia, in the 12th century, the high point of Khmer civilisation.
facts: It was built as a Hindu temple and later became a Buddhist one.
It appears on the flag of Cambodia.

landmark-047.summary: The world's largest Buddhist temple, built by the Sailendra dynasty in central Java, Indonesia, around the 9th century, a pilgrimage site whose tiers represent the stages toward enlightenment.
facts: Long forgotten, it was brought to the world's attention in 1814 by the British governor Raffles after he heard reports of it.
Up to 1,200 visitors a day may climb to the top, accompanied by a guide and wearing bamboo sandals.

landmark-048.summary: A pair of 452-metre skyscrapers in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, built by the national oil company and a symbol of the country's economic rise.
facts: They were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004.
Their floor plan is based on an eight-pointed Islamic star, and visitors can go up to the skybridge on the 41st floor.

landmark-049.summary: An integrated resort opened on Singapore's waterfront in 2010, whose ship-shaped garden atop three hotel towers has become a new symbol of the city.
facts: Its rooftop pool is about 190 meters above the ground and open only to hotel guests.
Every night, a light-and-water show called Spectra is staged on the bay in front.

landmark-050.summary: The royal temple within the Grand Palace in Bangkok, Thailand, home to the Emerald Buddha, the nation's guardian image, and the most sacred temple in the country.
facts: Despite its name, the Buddha is carved not from emerald but from green jade or jasper.
Three times a year, at each change of season, the king changes the statue's robes.

landmark-051.summary: A stretch of sea in Quang Ninh, northern Vietnam, studded with nearly 2,000 limestone islands and pillars, the country's signature seascape.
facts: Its name means “where the dragon descended.”
It became a World Natural Heritage Site in 1994.

landmark-052.summary: A volcano rising in a graceful cone on the border of Shizuoka and Yamanashi in central Honshu, Japan's highest peak and its national symbol.
facts: It stands 3,776 meters tall and was named a World Heritage Site in 2013 as a source of faith and artistic inspiration.
Hokusai's print of the mountain appears on the back of the new 1,000-yen note issued in 2024.

landmark-053.summary: A Zen temple in Kyoto, Japan, whose gold-leafed pavilion is reflected in a pond, a World Heritage Site emblematic of Muromachi-period aristocratic culture.
facts: The villa was acquired in 1397 by the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu; the temple's official name is Rokuon-ji.
A young monk burned it down in 1950; it was rebuilt in 1955, and Yukio Mishima turned the story into a novel.

landmark-054.summary: A 634-metre broadcasting tower opened in 2012 in Sumida, in Japan's capital, the tallest tower in the world and a new symbol of the city.
facts: The height of 634 is a pun on Musashi, the area's old province name.
It has observation decks at 350 and 450 meters and took over TV broadcasting from Tokyo Tower in 2013.

landmark-055.summary: The main royal palace, the first built by the Joseon dynasty in what is now Seoul, South Korea, in 1395, representing the dynasty's founding and Korean palace culture.
facts: Visitors wearing hanbok get in free.
Burned during the Imjin War in 1592, it lay empty for more than 270 years until it was rebuilt under King Gojong.

landmark-056.summary: A Silla-era temple on Mount Toham in Gyeongju, South Korea, built to bring the Buddhist ideal world down to earth, the pinnacle of Silla Buddhist art.
facts: The pagoda on the front of South Korea's 10-won coin is this temple's Dabotap.
In 1995, it became a World Heritage Site together with Seokguram Grotto.

landmark-057.summary: An observation and broadcasting structure on a hill in the heart of South Korea's capital, visible from almost anywhere in the city and its best-known landmark.
facts: It was completed as a transmission tower in 1975, but security concerns kept it closed to the public until 1980.
The love locks on the observation deck railings have become a famous sight.

landmark-058.summary: The world's tallest building at 828 metres, opened in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, in 2010, a symbol of the desert city's dazzling growth.
facts: On opening day, it was renamed from Burj Dubai in honor of the President of the United Arab Emirates.
The 163-story tower is where Tom Cruise scaled the outside wall himself in “Mission: Impossible.”

landmark-059.summary: The rock-cut capital of the Nabataean kingdom, carved into red sandstone cliffs in southern Jordan, named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World and a national symbol.
facts: At the end of a narrow gorge, Al-Khazneh, featured in “Indiana Jones,” comes into view.
It grew rich by charging tolls on caravans carrying frankincense and spices.

landmark-060.summary: The ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, begun by Darius I in the 6th century BC in southern Iran, whose palace ruins reflect the glory of an ancient empire.
facts: It was burned after Alexander the Great captured it in 330 BC.
Reliefs depicting processions of tribute bearers still survive.

landmark-061.summary: A 508-metre skyscraper opened in 2004 in northern Taiwan, shaped like segments of bamboo and built around the lucky number eight, a symbol of Taiwan.
facts: Its elevators climb more than 1,000 meters per minute.
Visitors can see the 660-ton steel damper ball suspended between the 88th and 92nd floors.

landmark-062.summary: The world's highest peak, rising 8,848.86 metres on the border of Nepal and China, the ultimate goal of mountaineers and a symbol of human endeavour.
facts: In 1977, Ko Sang-don became the first South Korean to stand on the summit.
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay made the first ascent in 1953.

landmark-063.summary: Giant stone tombs built for three pharaohs in the desert outside Cairo, Egypt, the enduring symbol of ancient Egyptian civilisation.
facts: They are the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.
Khufu's alone is thought to contain more than 2 million stone blocks.

landmark-064.summary: A reclining stone figure with a human head and a lion's body on the Giza Plateau, Egypt, the oldest known monumental sculpture in the country.
facts: It sits beside the pyramids, gazing east.
Its nose had already fallen off centuries before Napoleon's army arrived.

landmark-065.summary: Two rock-cut sanctuaries carved by Ramesses II into a cliff beside the Nile in southern Egypt in the 13th century BC, built to display the pharaoh's might to Nubia.
facts: Threatened with flooding by the construction of the Aswan High Dam in the 1960s, it was moved in its entirety and rebuilt.
Every year around February 22 and October 22, sunlight reaches the statues in its innermost sanctuary.

landmark-066.summary: A sanctuary on the east bank of the Nile in southern Egypt, in the ancient capital of Thebes, where the Opet Festival celebrated the renewal of royal power.
facts: One of its pair of obelisks now stands in Paris.
A 2.7-kilometer avenue of sphinxes once linked it to the Karnak Temple.

landmark-067.summary: Africa's highest peak at 5,895 metres, a snow-capped volcano near the equator in northeastern Tanzania and a symbol of the continent.
facts: Trails lead to the top without technical climbing skills, so tens of thousands attempt it every year.
It is the tallest free-standing mountain in the world.

landmark-068.summary: A vast savanna in northern Tanzania, stage for the world's largest land mammal migration as over a million wildebeest move each year.
facts: Its name means “endless plains.”
It forms a single ecosystem with Kenya's Maasai Mara.

landmark-069.summary: A national reserve in southwestern Kenya on the Tanzanian border, rich in lions, leopards and elephants, and East Africa's best-known safari destination.
facts: “Mara” means “spotted” in the Maasai language.
From July to October, safari vehicles flock to watch herds of wildebeest cross the Mara River.

landmark-070.summary: The remains of an ancient maritime power near Tunis, Tunisia, the centre of Phoenician civilisation that fought Rome for control of the Mediterranean.
facts: It fell to Rome in 146 BC, at the end of the third of the Punic Wars.
Founded by Phoenicians from Tyre, its name means “New City.”

landmark-071.summary: A great open marketplace in Marrakesh, Morocco, where storytellers, musicians and snake charmers keep oral traditions alive on a living stage.
facts: It is the central square of the medina, the old quarter of Marrakesh.
In 2001, UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity.

landmark-072.summary: A flat-topped rock massif rising behind Cape Town, South Africa, the symbol of the city and one of the New7Wonders of Nature.
facts: The summit stands 1,085 meters high and can be reached by cable car.
The white cloud that spills over the top is called the “tablecloth.”

landmark-073.summary: A rocky headland on South Africa's southwestern coast, a symbol of the Age of Discovery that heralded the opening of the sea route from Europe to India.
facts: Bartolomeu Dias first reached it in 1488 and named it the Cape of Storms.
Africa's southernmost point is actually Cape Agulhas.

landmark-074.summary: The stone-built capital of a kingdom raised by ancestors of the Shona in southern Africa between the 11th and 15th centuries, the largest ancient stone ruins south of the Sahara.
facts: The country's name and the bird emblem on its flag both come from these ruins.
Its walls were built of fitted stones without any mortar.

landmark-075.summary: A colossal sculpture in New York Harbor given by France to mark the centennial of American independence, a symbol of democracy that greeted generations of immigrants.
facts: It was unveiled in 1886, and its internal iron framework was designed by Gustave Eiffel.
The tablet in its left hand is inscribed with the date of the Declaration of Independence.

landmark-076.summary: A vast red gorge carved by the Colorado River in Arizona, USA, sacred to Native American peoples and one of the country's iconic natural landscapes.
facts: In places, it is more than 1,800 meters deep.
Its rock layers record nearly 2 billion years of Earth's history.

landmark-077.summary: A red suspension span crossing the strait at the mouth of San Francisco Bay, USA, the symbol of San Francisco and the American West.
facts: It opened in 1937, and its anti-rust primer, “International Orange,” was kept as its final color.
With a 1,280-meter main span, it was the world's longest suspension bridge until 1964.

landmark-078.summary: The residence and workplace of the US president in Washington, D.C., since 1800, a symbol of the American government and presidential power.
facts: In 1901, Theodore Roosevelt made “White House” its official name.
The president's office, the Oval Office, is in the West Wing.

landmark-079.summary: A sculpture of four presidents' faces carved into a granite cliff in South Dakota, USA, chosen to represent the nation's birth, growth, development and preservation.
facts: It is the setting of the final chase scene in Hitchcock's “North by Northwest.”
About 400 people worked on it, and most of the rock was removed with dynamite.

landmark-080.summary: A vast volcanic region centred on Wyoming, USA, full of geysers and hot springs, and the world's first example of a nationally protected natural area.
facts: It was designated a national park in 1872.
Old Faithful geyser shoots water to an average height of about 44 meters roughly every 90 minutes.

landmark-081.summary: A 553-metre observation and broadcast spire on Lake Ontario in Toronto, Canada, built by the national railway company and now a symbol of the city and country.
facts: It has an observation level with a glass floor.
After opening in 1976, it was the world's tallest free-standing structure until 2007.

landmark-082.summary: An area of jade lakes and glaciers in the Rocky Mountains of Alberta, Canada, the first natural area in the country to be protected by the state.
facts: Lake Louise gets its turquoise color from glacial rock flour.
Railway workers found hot springs here in 1883, and after disputes over who owned them, the area became a protected reserve in 1885.

landmark-083.summary: The ruins of a Maya city on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, one of the greatest cities of the late Maya civilisation and one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.
facts: At the spring and fall equinoxes, a serpent-shaped shadow appears on its stairway.
Its four stairways of 91 steps each, plus the top platform, add up to 365.

landmark-084.summary: An ancient city northeast of Mexico City, lined with the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, once the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas and a centre of Mesoamerican civilisation.
facts: It had already been abandoned by the time the Aztecs discovered it.
Its central avenue is called the Avenue of the Dead.

landmark-085.summary: A lock-based artificial waterway across the Central American isthmus linking the Pacific and Atlantic, a shortcut for world shipping and a symbol of 20th-century engineering.
facts: Opened in 1914, it spared ships the long voyage around Cape Horn at the tip of South America.
New locks opened in 2016 to let larger ships through.

landmark-086.summary: A stone citadel built by an Inca emperor on an Andean ridge in Peru in the mid-15th century, the iconic "lost city" of Inca civilisation.
facts: It sits at about 2,430 meters above sea level, and the number of visitors allowed each day is capped.
It became widely known to the outside world in 1911 through Hiram Bingham.

landmark-087.summary: Giant figures of animals and geometric shapes drawn on the desert floor of southern Peru by an ancient people, thought to be ritual in purpose and now a World Heritage Site.
facts: Hard to make out from the ground, they became known to the world in the 1920s and '30s when planes flew over them.
They have survived so long because it almost never rains there.

landmark-088.summary: A colossal figure of Jesus with outstretched arms overlooking Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, a symbol of the country and of its Catholic faith.
facts: It stands on the summit of Corcovado mountain.
Completed in 1931, it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.

landmark-089.summary: The dried bed of an ancient lake on the Andean plateau of southwestern Bolivia, a white crust of salt that mirrors the sky after rain.
facts: It is the largest salt flat in the world.
It holds the world's largest deposits of lithium, used in batteries for electric cars and smartphones.

landmark-090.summary: Giant stone figures with human faces carved by the Rapa Nui people of Easter Island, Chile, to honour their deified ancestors, the symbol of the island.
facts: More than 900 statues have been found on the island so far.
Most were carved from volcanic tuff at Rano Raraku.

landmark-091.summary: A volcanic archipelago in the Pacific off Ecuador where Darwin found clues to his theory of evolution, often called a living laboratory of evolution.
facts: The finches on each island have differently shaped beaks.
Giant tortoises and marine iguanas live here.

landmark-092.summary: The cascade with the world's greatest drop, plunging from a tabletop mountain in southeastern Venezuela, the emblem of Canaima National Park, a World Heritage Site.
facts: It drops 979 meters and inspired Paradise Falls in the movie “Up.”
It is named after aviator Jimmie Angel, who first flew over it in 1933.

landmark-093.summary: A performing arts centre opened in 1973 on a harbour point in Australia's largest city, whose sail-like roof makes it a masterpiece of 20th-century architecture and a symbol of the country.
facts: It was designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon, who resigned in 1966 and never saw it completed.
The more than 1.05 million tiles covering its white roofs were made by a Swedish company.

landmark-094.summary: A huge sandstone monolith rising alone from the desert of Australia's Northern Territory, the red rock that symbolises the heart of the continent.
facts: It is sacred to the Aboriginal Anangu people and is also known as Ayers Rock, a name given by an explorer in 1873.
Climbing it has been banned since October 2019.

landmark-095.summary: The world's largest coral system, off the coast of Queensland, Australia, home to countless marine species and a natural World Heritage Site since 1981.
facts: It stretches for 2,300 kilometers.
When water temperatures rise, the corals turn white and die in a process called bleaching.

landmark-096.summary: A fiord in Fiordland National Park on New Zealand's South Island, where glacier-carved cliffs and rainforest make it the country's best-known natural attraction.
facts: It rains so often that waterfalls form on every cliff face.
Rudyard Kipling called it the eighth wonder of the world.
